questions.q:
Which of the following collections is a set? Justify your answer in one sentence.
(i) The collection of all prime numbers less than 20.
(ii) The collection of all difficult chapters in the Class 11 Mathematics textbook.
questions.a: (i) is a set because "prime number less than 20" is a precise mathematical property — we can definitively check any number. (ii) is not a set because "difficult" is subjective and varies from student to student; there is no objective rule to decide membership. A wrong answer here reveals the student thinks any named group is a set, missing the "well-defined" requirement.

questions.q: A student writes: "Let S be the set of all integers x such that x² < 10." Another student says: "That's not a set because it has infinite elements." Who is correct? Explain why.
questions.a: The first student is correct. The collection is a set because the rule "x² < 10" is well-defined — we can test any integer. The number of elements (finite or infinite) does not determine whether something is a set; only the clarity of the membership rule matters. A wrong answer reveals confusion between "well-defined" and "finite" — students often think infinite collections cannot be sets.

questions.q: Let A = {x : x is a letter in the word "MATHEMATICS"}. Write A in roster form. Then state whether 'T' ∈ A and 'Z' ∈ A are true or false.
questions.a: A = {M, A, T, H, E, I, C, S}. Note: letters are distinct, so 'M', 'A', 'T' appear once each. 'T' ∈ A is true (T appears in MATHEMATICS). 'Z' ∈ A is false (Z does not appear). A wrong answer reveals two possible errors: (a) repeating letters in roster form (violating "distinct"), or (b) not understanding that ∈ checks membership in the final set, not in the original word with repetitions.

C₁ and C₂ are sets because their defining properties ("factor of 12" and "multiple of 12") are precise and unambiguous for any natural number. C₃ is not a set because "large" has no fixed mathematical definition — it is relative and subjective. The distinguishing property is **objective decidability**: for C₁ and C₂, there is an algorithm to test membership; for C₃, there is not. A wrong answer reveals the student cannot articulate the precise meaning of "well-defined" beyond vague language.

questions.q: A textbook claims: "The collection of all sets is a set." Evaluate this statement. Is it true or false? Defend your answer using the definition of a set.
questions.a: The statement is false. If "the collection of all sets" were a set, it would have to be a member of itself, leading to Russell's Paradox (a set that contains all sets that do not contain themselves). More simply at Class 11 level: the phrase "all sets" does not provide a well-defined membership rule that can be applied without contradiction — it is self-referential and ill-defined. A wrong answer reveals the student treats "collection" and "set" as synonyms without checking the well-defined criterion.

questions.q: Create your own example of a collection that is NOT a set, and another that IS a set. Both must be from real-life contexts (not pure math). For each, write the membership rule explicitly and explain why it passes or fails the "well-defined" test.
questions.a: Example of a set: "The collection of all students in Class 11A who have a roll number ≤ 30." Rule: x ∈ S iff x is a student in Class 11A AND roll number ≤ 30. This is well-defined because roll numbers are unique, objective, and verifiable. Example of a non-set: "The collection of all tall students in Class 11A." Rule: x ∈ T iff x is a student in Class 11A AND x is tall. This fails because "tall" has no fixed threshold — 170 cm might be tall to one person, not to another. A poor answer uses vague rules like "good students" or "important books" without recognizing the subjectivity.
